title: AI Datasets
answer: Training and evaluation datasets with size, licence, provenance, language coverage, and documented bias.

reading.body:
AI datasets are documented by three properties: what they contain, what they measure, and what may lawfully be done with them.

The structure separates training corpora from evaluation sets from licensing and provenance. That split matters because the three fail differently. A training corpus can be large and still unusable if its licence does not permit the intended use. An evaluation set can be well licensed and still measure the wrong thing. Provenance is the thread that runs through all three, since it is what lets a buyer or a researcher tell which of the other two properties actually holds.

For AI specifically, the constraint this data describes is legal and documentary rather than physical. Compute, buildings, and power set the ceiling on what can be trained. Datasets and their licences set what is permitted to be trained on, and a model's capability claims are only as good as the benchmarks behind them. The three child areas are the places where that permission and that measurement get established.

What this data does not contain is any dataset itself. There are no sizes, no licence names, no language counts, and no bias findings, only the categories under which those facts would be filed. It also carries no dates for when any dataset was created or revised. A reader should treat it as a map of where to look, not as a record of what is there.
